passages.t: ‘O foolish Galatians’: how did you receive the Spirit?
passages.happening:
Paul turns from his story to the Galatians themselves. “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified” (verse 1).

Then he asks one question, in several forms. “I would like to learn just one thing from you: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?” (verse 2). “Are you so foolish? After starting in the Spirit, are you now finishing in the flesh?” (verse 3). Have they suffered so much for nothing (verse 4)? “Does God lavish His Spirit on you and work miracles among you because you practice the law, or because you hear and believe?” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
‘Foolish’ here means not thinking, not using the sense you have. Paul is not calling them stupid. He is saying they have forgotten what they saw.

‘Bewitched’ is a word linked with the evil eye, the widespread belief that a jealous look could put a spell on someone. Paul uses it with irony: you are acting as if someone had cast a spell on you.

‘Clearly portrayed’ was used for a public notice posted for everyone to read. When Paul preached, he set the crucified Christ before them as plainly as a poster on a wall. They did not need anything more.

Then comes Paul's strongest evidence. The Galatians had received the Spirit. Something had happened among them: changed lives, joy, even miracles (verse 5). And it happened when they heard the message and believed, before anyone told them about circumcision. If God had already welcomed them, how could circumcision be needed to make them belong?

‘Starting in the Spirit’ and ‘finishing in the flesh’ is the heart of the chapter. ‘Flesh’ here means human effort, and also the body cut in circumcision. Paul's point is that the Christian life does not begin by grace and then continue by our own work. It is grace from start to finish.

‘Suffered’ in verse 4 may mean that they had suffered for their faith, as the churches in the south did when Paul first came (Acts 14:22). It can also mean ‘experienced’, all the good things God had done among them. Either way, Paul asks: was it all for nothing?
passages.ot:
The prophets promised that God would one day pour out his Spirit on his people. Through Isaiah God said, “I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring” (Isaiah 44:3). Through Joel, “I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28).

For Paul, the Spirit given to Gentile believers was the sign that those promises were being kept. The same Spirit came to Gentiles in the house of Cornelius, and Peter said at once that they should be baptized (Acts 10:44-48). It was the evidence that settled the question.
passages.asks: Paul asks the Galatians to remember how their life with God began. Ask how yours began, if it has. Was it something you earned, or something you received? And ask whether you are trying to finish by your own effort what God started by grace: as if the Christian life were a free gift at the door and hard wages after.

passages.happening:
Paul goes to Abraham, the father of Israel. “So also, ‘Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness’” (verse 6). “Understand, then, that those who have faith are sons of Abraham” (verse 7).

Scripture saw it coming. “The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham: ‘All nations will be blessed through you’” (verse 8). “So those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The teachers in Galatia surely spoke about Abraham. He was the first to be circumcised, and the covenant sign was given to him. To be a true child of Abraham, they likely said, you must be circumcised as he was.

Paul goes back further in Abraham's story. Before Abraham was circumcised, God promised him a family as many as the stars, and Abraham believed. God counted that trust as righteousness. Only later did circumcision come, as a sign (Genesis 17). So Abraham's standing with God began with faith.

‘Credited’ is a word from keeping accounts. Something was written down to Abraham's account that he had not earned. He trusted God's promise, and God counted him in the right.

‘Sons of Abraham’ means the true family of Abraham, those who share his likeness. Paul's point is that the family is marked by trust in God, not by birth or by circumcision.

Verse 8 says the Scripture ‘foretold the gospel to Abraham’. The good news was not a new idea. It was there in God's first promise: through Abraham, all nations would be blessed. Gentiles coming to God by faith is not a change of plan. It is the plan.
passages.ot:
Paul's first text is Genesis 15:6. God took Abram outside and told him to count the stars: “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5). Then, “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Abram had no son, and his body was old. He trusted God anyway.

His second text is God's first promise to Abram: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). God repeated it later: “through him all the nations of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis 18:18). Paul's wording blends these promises.

The note on Genesis 15 in this Study Bible takes up Abram's trust in its own setting.
passages.asks: Abraham believed God when everything he could see said the promise was impossible. Ask what God has promised in Scripture that you find hard to believe. And ask who you think of as truly belonging to God's family. Paul says the family is marked by trust in God's promise, not by background.

passages.t: Christ became a curse for us
passages.happening:
“All who rely on works of the law are under a curse” (verse 10). Paul quotes the law: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law” (verse 10).

He goes on. “Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because, ‘The righteous will live by faith’” (verse 11). But the law works another way: “The man who does these things will live by them” (verse 12).

Then comes the answer. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree’” (verse 13). He did this “in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
These are among the hardest verses in Paul. Take them slowly.

The law of Moses ended with blessings for obeying and curses for disobeying (Deuteronomy 27 and 28). The curses were not God's spite. They were the warning that came with the covenant. Israel's own history, as the prophets told it, was a history of falling under those curses, through exile and loss.

Paul says that relying on the law as the way to stand right with God puts a person under that curse, because the law requires everything. Nobody does everything.

Then he sets two texts side by side. The law says life comes to the one who does what it commands (Leviticus 18:5). The prophet says the righteous will live by faith (Habakkuk 2:4). Paul hears in them two different ways of standing before God: doing, and trusting.

Verse 13 is the turning point. ‘Redeemed’ was the word for buying back a slave or a prisoner. Christ bought us out from under the curse, and he did it by taking it on himself. The law said that a body hung on a tree was under God's curse. Jesus died on a Roman cross, a tree. So the one who never broke the law took the law's curse on himself.

And it was all for a purpose: so that Abraham's blessing would reach the Gentiles, and all who believe would receive the Spirit. The cross is where God kept his promise to Abraham.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes four texts. The first is Deuteronomy 27:26. In the BSB, which translates the Hebrew, it reads, “Cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice” (Deuteronomy 27:26). Paul's wording, with ‘everyone’ and ‘everything’, is close to the old Greek translation that most of his hearers knew.

The second is Habakkuk 2:4: “the righteous will live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4). In Habakkuk, God is answering a prophet who cannot understand why evil seems to win. The answer is to wait for God, trusting him. Paul takes the line as the pattern for life with God.

The third is Leviticus 18:5: “the man who does these things will live by them” (Leviticus 18:5). In Leviticus this is good news for Israel: God's ways are the way of life.

The fourth is Deuteronomy 21:23. When a man was executed, his body could be hung on a tree for all to see, but it had to be buried before night, “because anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse” (Deuteronomy 21:23). By Paul's day, Jews had come to connect this verse with crucifixion.
passages.hard:
What does Paul mean when he says Christ became ‘a curse for us’?

He does not mean that Jesus was wicked, or that God stopped loving his Son. Paul says Christ ‘redeemed us’ by taking our place. The curse that hung over those who broke God's law fell on him instead. Christians have always seen here something of what happened on the cross: the one who had no sin bore the consequence of ours.

Christians describe what the cross achieved in more than one way. Many, especially in churches of the Reformation, read these verses as substitution: Christ bore the penalty that sinners deserved. Others stress Christ's victory: by entering the curse he broke its power, as he broke the power of death. Others stress that he did it to set people free, as one buys a slave out of slavery. Many hold these pictures together. The site's note on Romans 3:21-26 sets out the main ways Christians describe the cross, and the note on 2 Corinthians 5:18-21 says more about the great exchange. These notes do not choose between them.

What all share is this. The cross was not a defeat that God made the best of. It was God's own act of love, in which the Son gave himself freely. The Nicene Creed confesses that he was crucified ‘for us’. And its purpose reaches far beyond one people: the blessing of Abraham comes to the nations.

Some have used verses like these to claim that the law itself was a curse, or that Jews were cursed. Paul says neither. The law is holy (Romans 7:12). Christ redeemed ‘us’, and Paul, a Jew, counts himself among those who needed it.
passages.asks: Paul says Christ took the curse that was ours. Ask what you still carry as if it had not been taken: guilt for something confessed, shame for something forgiven. And ask why God did it: so that the blessing would reach people who were far off. Who is far off from you, whom God means to bless?

passages.happening:
“Brothers, let me put this in human terms. Even a human covenant, once it is ratified, cannot be canceled or amended” (verse 15).

God's promises were spoken to Abraham “and to his seed” (verse 16). Paul notes that the word is singular, “meaning One, who is Christ” (verse 16).

Then his main point: “The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God, so as to nullify the promise” (verse 17). If the inheritance came by the law, it would not come by promise. Instead, “God freely granted it to Abraham through a promise” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Paul uses a picture from everyday life. Once an agreement or a will is signed and sealed, no one else can come along later and change its terms. The Greek word for covenant can also mean a will.

God made his promise to Abraham long before the law came at Mount Sinai. So the law, coming later, cannot add new conditions to that promise. If it did, the promise would no longer be a promise. It would be a contract.

The number 430 comes from Exodus, which counts the time Israel spent in Egypt. Paul uses it to show how long the promise stood before the law came. The old Greek translation counts the 430 years from Abraham's time in Canaan, which fits Paul's count exactly. His point does not hang on the number: the law came long after the promise.

‘Inheritance’ is what a child receives from a father, not what a worker earns from an employer. Paul's language is family language. God's blessing is given, not paid.
passages.ot:
God's promise was made to Abraham ‘and to his offspring’. God told him, “all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever” (Genesis 13:15). After Abraham offered Isaac, God said, “through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). The BSB uses ‘offspring’ in Genesis and ‘seed’ in Galatians; they translate the same idea.

The 430 years come from Exodus: “Now the duration of the Israelites’ stay in Egypt was 430 years” (Exodus 12:40).

God also promised David a single offspring who would reign: “I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:12). Christians have long read that promise as fulfilled in Christ.
passages.hard:
Is Paul's argument about ‘seed’ and ‘seeds’ fair?

The word for seed, in Hebrew and in Greek, is like the English word ‘offspring’. It can mean one child or many descendants. Paul knows this. In verse 29 he says that all who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed, using the word for many. His point in verse 16 is that the promise to Abraham's offspring comes to its focus in one person, the Messiah, and through him reaches the many who belong to him.

Reading Scripture closely, word by word, was common among Jewish teachers of Paul's day, and Paul uses that way of reading here. He is not saying the word could only ever mean one person. He is saying that, read in the light of Christ, the promise always pointed to him, as God's promise to David pointed to one king. The people of God are gathered into the one Son.
passages.asks: God's promise to Abraham could not be cancelled by anything that came later. Ask whether you trust God's promises as gifts, or treat them as deals with conditions you must keep. And ask what it means that you are an heir, not a worker, in God's house.

passages.t: Why the law? A guardian until Christ came
passages.happening:
If the promise came first, why give the law at all? “Why then was the law given? It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred” (verse 19). It came through angels, by a go-between (verses 19-20).

Is the law against God's promises? “Certainly not!” (verse 21). No law could give life. Instead, “the Scripture pronounces all things confined by sin, so that by faith in Jesus Christ the promise might be given to those who believe” (verse 22).

Before faith came, “we were held in custody under the law” (verse 23). “So the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (verse 24). “Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Paul has to answer an obvious objection. If the promise does everything, was the law a mistake? His answer is no. The law had a real job, given by God, for a time.

‘Added because of transgressions’ can mean two things that fit together. The law named sin as wrong-doing, breaking a known command. And it held sin in check, guarding Israel until the promise came.

The guardian, in Greek paidagōgos, was a household slave in Greek and Roman families. He looked after a boy, walked him to school, kept him out of trouble and disciplined him until he came of age. He was not the father and not the teacher. And once the boy grew up, he no longer needed one. Paul says the law was like that for Israel: protective, strict, and for a season. Now that Christ has come, God's people have come of age.

‘Through angels’ reflects a Jewish tradition that angels were present when God gave the law at Sinai. Stephen says the same in Acts 7:53. Paul's point is that the law came through go-betweens, while the promise came from God directly.

Verse 20 is one of the hardest sentences in Paul, and readers have suggested many meanings. The most common is that a go-between stands between two parties, but the promise was God's alone. God is one, and he made his promise by himself.
passages.ot:
The law was given at Sinai with great glory. Moses later said, “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned upon us from Seir; He shone forth from Mount Paran and came with myriads of holy ones” (Deuteronomy 33:2). The tradition of angels at Sinai grew from verses like this.

The law was given to a people already rescued. God said to Israel at Sinai, “if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations” (Exodus 19:5). The law did not make Israel God's people. It shaped the life of a people God had already freed.

And Scripture's verdict that all are ‘confined by sin’ is the verdict of the psalms Paul gathers in Romans 3, such as “there is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 14:3).
passages.asks: A guardian is good for a child and wrong for a grown son. Ask whether you relate to God more like a child under rules, anxious to stay out of trouble, or like a son at home. And ask what the law still teaches you, about God and about yourself, now that it points you to Christ.

passages.happening:
“You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus” (verse 26). “For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (verse 27).

“There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (verse 28).

“And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
‘Sons of God’ includes daughters. In Paul's world sons were the heirs, and Paul wants every believer, man or woman, slave or free, to hear that they have the full rights of an heir in God's family.

‘Clothed yourselves with Christ’ is a picture of putting on new clothes. People in the ancient world knew that clothes showed who you were: your rank, your people, whether you were slave or free. Paul says that in baptism believers put on Christ. That is now the first thing about them.

Verse 28 names three divisions that shaped all of life in Paul's world. Jew and Greek: the line between Israel and the nations. Slave and free: the line of status and power. Male and female: the line of sex. The last pair is worded differently in Greek, ‘no male and female’, the exact words of Genesis 1:27 in the old Greek. Many readers think Paul is pointing to the new creation in Christ.

Notice what Paul is answering. In Galatia some said that Gentiles needed something more to belong fully. Paul says that in Christ no believer is second class. Everyone who belongs to Christ is Abraham's seed and an heir.

Paul did not mean that these differences simply vanish. In his letters he still speaks to Jews and Gentiles, to slaves and masters, to husbands and wives. But none of these is the ground of a person's standing with God, and none decides who may sit at the table.
passages.ot:
‘Male and female’ comes from the creation story: “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). Both are made in God's image.

Being clothed by God is a picture from the prophets: “He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10).

And God's first promise to Abraham already reached across the line between peoples: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3).
passages.hard:
Two questions come up in these verses.

First, baptism (verse 27). All Christians agree that Paul speaks of baptism here as joining a person to Christ, and that faith and baptism belong together in the New Testament. Churches differ on how baptism works and who should receive it. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians hold that God truly gives new life in baptism, and they baptize infants. Reformed and Presbyterian churches hold that baptism is a sign and seal of God's covenant promise, and they also baptize the children of believers. Baptists and many other evangelicals hold that baptism is the believer's public sign of a faith already given, and they baptize those old enough to confess it. The site's note on Acts 2:37-41 sets out these views in their holders' own terms. These notes do not choose.

Second, verse 28. What all agree on is the plain point: in Christ there is no second-class believer. Jew and Gentile, slave and free, man and woman stand on the same ground before God, as children and heirs. That is not a small thing. In Paul's world each of those lines decided where a person could sit, what they could own, and whose voice counted.

Christians have drawn on this verse in many debates. In the long fight against slavery, many pointed to it. And churches differ today on what it means for men and women in the church and the home. Complementarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth before God, and that God has given them different roles, with the office of pastor or elder given to qualified men; they read this verse as speaking of equal standing in salvation, while other passages govern roles. Egalitarian Christians believe that every role in the church is open to both, as God gifts them, and they read this verse as a principle that reaches into the life of the church. These are views held by faithful believers. These notes do not choose between them. The site's note on Acts 18:24-28 sets out both more fully.

Both agree on something that matters greatly: no reading of this verse gives anyone licence to treat another believer as worth less, or to use power over them.
passages.asks: Paul names the three lines that most divided his world, and says that in Christ none of them decides who belongs. Ask which lines divide your world: race, class, politics, education, sex. Ask which of them you quietly use to decide who is really one of you. And if you belong to Christ, ask what it means that you are an heir, with nothing added.
